power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

Contemporary changes in work have been characterized by intensified demands alongside greater expectations for employees to autonomously organize their work and pursue work-related goals (Mauno et al., 2023; Niazi et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Contemporary changes in work have been characterized by intensified demands alongside greater expectations for employees to autonomously organize their work and pursue work-related goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Mauno et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Niazi et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Meeting occupational demands involves regulatory processes such as maintaining attention, organizing and prioritizing tasks, managing time, and sustaining goal-directed behavior.

These processes may be particularly relevant to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), given documented difficulties in attention and executive functioning and their associations with occupational functioning (Chan & Langberg, 2024; Fuermaier et al., 2021; Turjeman-Levi et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These processes may be particularly relevant to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), given documented difficulties in attention and executive functioning and their associations with occupational functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chan & Langberg, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Fuermaier et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Turjeman-Levi et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although ADHD is clinically diagnosed categorically, its core symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity are dimensionally distributed, with evidence suggesting continuity rather than a discrete boundary between affected and unaffected individuals (Arildskov et al., 2022; McLennan, 2016).
text.formatted: Although ADHD is clinically diagnosed categorically, its core symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity are dimensionally distributed, with evidence suggesting continuity rather than a discrete boundary between affected and unaffected individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arildskov et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">McLennan, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This dimensional perspective is also compatible with the neurodiversity paradigm, which situates neurodevelopmental differences within broader variation in human neurocognitive functioning rather than treating diagnostic categories as necessarily reflecting qualitatively distinct populations (Doyle & McDowall, 2022; Koi, 2021).
text.formatted: This dimensional perspective is also compatible with the neurodiversity paradigm, which situates neurodevelopmental differences within broader variation in human neurocognitive functioning rather than treating diagnostic categories as necessarily reflecting qualitatively distinct populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Doyle & McDowall, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Koi, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, ADHD-related characteristics may be relevant to occupational functioning beyond clinically diagnosed populations.

ADHD has been associated with occupational underattainment and impaired work functioning (Biederman et al., 2008; Brook et al., 2013), while functional impairment has also been documented at subthreshold symptom levels (Hong et al., 2014) and in relation to ADHD symptoms in community samples without established diagnoses (Fuermaier et al., 2021).
text.formatted: ADHD has been associated with occupational underattainment and impaired work functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Biederman et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Brook et al., 2013)</ref>, while functional impairment has also been documented at subthreshold symptom levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hong et al., 2014)</ref> and in relation to ADHD symptoms in community samples without established diagnoses <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fuermaier et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the occupational relevance of ADHD, workplace-specific research remains comparatively limited, particularly regarding how adults with ADHD-related characteristics manage occupational demands in everyday work contexts (Lauder et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Despite the occupational relevance of ADHD, workplace-specific research remains comparatively limited, particularly regarding how adults with ADHD-related characteristics manage occupational demands in everyday work contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lauder et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Among adults with ADHD, research has identified diverse self-developed compensatory strategies involving attention, organization, adaptation, and external support (Canela et al., 2017; Kysow et al., 2017), while qualitative research among working adults with ADHD has described extending work into evenings and weekends in response to difficulties encountered during regular working hours (Oscarsson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Among adults with ADHD, research has identified diverse self-developed compensatory strategies involving attention, organization, adaptation, and external support <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Canela et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kysow et al., 2017)</ref>, while qualitative research among working adults with ADHD has described extending work into evenings and weekends in response to difficulties encountered during regular working hours <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Oscarsson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Workaholism, procrastination, perfectionism, and taking on excessive numbers of tasks have likewise been discussed in relation to ADHD and increased work investment (Andreassen et al., 2016; Oscarsson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Workaholism, procrastination, perfectionism, and taking on excessive numbers of tasks have likewise been discussed in relation to ADHD and increased work investment <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andreassen et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Oscarsson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, such responses are not inherently self-endangering.
However, some may overlap with forms of self-endangering work behavior (SEWB) when maintaining occupational functioning involves additional investment of time, effort, or recovery resources.
ADHD-related characteristics have likewise been associated with occupational strain, including greater stress and burnout (Erdal et al., 2025).
text.formatted: ADHD-related characteristics have likewise been associated with occupational strain, including greater stress and burnout <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Erdal et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: SEWB describes forms of work behavior through which employees attempt to maintain occupational functioning despite potential costs to health and recovery (Dettmers et al., 2016; Krause et al., 2015; Mustafić et al., 2023).
text.formatted: SEWB describes forms of work behavior through which employees attempt to maintain occupational functioning despite potential costs to health and recovery <ref type="bibr">(Dettmers et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Krause et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Mustafić et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It encompasses diverse strategies, including extending and intensifying work, working despite illness, sacrificing recovery, using substances to maintain performance or facilitate recovery, reducing work quality, and concealing performance difficulties (Dettmers et al., 2016).
text.formatted: It encompasses diverse strategies, including extending and intensifying work, working despite illness, sacrificing recovery, using substances to maintain performance or facilitate recovery, reducing work quality, and concealing performance difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dettmers et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: SEWB therefore provides a framework for examining not only whether employees experience difficulties at work, but also whether the strategies accompanying continued occupational functioning may themselves have implications for well-being.
A compensatory-regulation perspective provides a theoretical rationale for linking ADHD-related characteristics with SEWB.

Difficulties with attention regulation, organization, prioritization, or time management may increase the regulatory demands involved in attaining occupational goals (Chan & Langberg, 2024; Turjeman-Levi et al., 2024). Hockey's (1997) compensatory control framework proposes that when demands threaten performance goals, individuals may maintain performance by mobilizing additional effort or reallocating resources, potentially at increased personal cost.
text.formatted: Difficulties with attention regulation, organization, prioritization, or time management may increase the regulatory demands involved in attaining occupational goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chan & Langberg, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Turjeman-Levi et al., 2024</ref>). <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hockey's (1997)</ref> compensatory control framework proposes that when demands threaten performance goals, individuals may maintain performance by mobilizing additional effort or reallocating resources, potentially at increased personal cost.

text.text: Applied to ADHDrelated occupational difficulties, this framework suggests that maintaining work goals may under some circumstances involve additional investment of time, effort, or recovery resources and thereby overlap with particular forms of SEWB.

This does not imply that SEWB among workers with elevated ADHD symptoms necessarily represents compensation for ADHD-related difficulties; rather, compensatory regulation provides a theoretical rationale for examining whether ADHD-related characteristics are associated with greater or different forms of SEWB.
This question is relevant to occupational health because strategies that help maintain functioning in the short term may be associated with strain.

Working longer and more intensively has predicted subsequent increases in time pressure and unfinished tasks (Baethge et al., 2026; Ganster et al., 2018), while SEWB has been associated with emotional exhaustion, fatigue, and psychosomatic complaints (Deci et al., 2016; Mustafić et al., 2023) and may partly account for associations between work demands and exhaustion (Knecht et al., 2017).

text.text: At the same time, SEWB comprises conceptually distinct behaviours that may differ in their associations with occupational well-being.
It also remains unclear whether these associations are comparable across workers with differing ADHD-related characteristics.

Continuous ADHD symptoms were assessed using the full 18-item ASRS v1.1.
Items were rated on a five-point response scale ranging from "never" to "very often."
Mean scores were calculated separately for inattention (9 items) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (9 items), with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.

Ten dimensions were assessed: recovery sacrifice, quality reduction, presenteeism, performance-enhancing substance use, work during leisure time/constant availability, work intensification, quality deficits, concealment of performance problems, reduced exchange with colleagues, and skipping breaks.
Subscale scores were calculated as item means, with higher scores indicating greater engagement in the respective form of SEWB.
Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω.
Reliability estimates across the ten dimensions ranged from α = .59 to .95 and ω = .64 to .95.

Analyses were conducted using the final analytical sample of 471 participants.
To address RQ1, differences in the ten SEWB dimensions between the ADHD and comparison groups were examined using Welch independent-samples t tests.
P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons across the ten SEWB dimensions using the Holm method, and Cohen's d was reported as an effect-size measure.
Bivariate correlations and variance inflation factors (VIFs) were examined to assess multicollinearity among the SEWB dimensions.
An observed-variable path model was estimated in R using the lavaan package.
ADHD group membership was modeled as a predictor of each of the ten SEWB dimensions.

ADHD group membership and the ten SEWB dimensions were then simultaneously modeled as predictors of emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, reduced personal accomplishment, work engagement, and perceived stress.
Age and sex were included as covariates.
Age was meancentered, and sex was dummy-coded with female as the reference category.
The model was estimated using robust maximum likelihood (MLR), with missing data handled using fullinformation maximum likelihood (FIML).

To address RQ2, latent profile analysis (LPA) was conducted using the two continuous ADHD symptom dimensions (inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity) and the ten SEWB dimensions as profile indicators.
All 12 indicators were standardized prior to analysis.

Candidate solutions containing one through six profiles were initially estimated in R using the tidyLPA package, with indicator variances constrained to equality across profiles and within-profile covariances fixed to zero.

Solutions were evaluated based on the Akaike information criterion (AIC), Bayesian information criterion (BIC), sample-size-adjusted BIC (SABIC), entropy, profile size, and substantive interpretability.

Because the information criteria continued to improve as additional profiles were extracted, alternative solutions allowing indicator variances to vary across profiles while retaining zero within-profile covariances were examined.

As a robustness analysis, Gaussian finite-mixture models were additionally estimated using the mclust package, comparing equal-variance (EEI) and profile-specific diagonalvariance (VVI) covariance structures across one-through six-profile solutions.
The final solution was selected based on statistical fit, classification precision, profile size, parsimony, and substantive distinctiveness.
Posterior probabilities and classification uncertainty were examined to evaluate classification quality.

To address RQ3, the identified ADHD-SEWB profiles were compared on emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, reduced personal accomplishment, work engagement, and perceived stress using separate linear regression models.
Profile membership was entered as a categorical predictor, with mean-centered age and sex included as covariates; sex was dummy-coded with female as the reference category.
Analyses included participants with available data for the respective outcome.
Because profile sizes were unequal, heteroskedasticity-consistent HC3 covariance estimates were used.
Overall profile effects were evaluated using Type II robust tests implemented with the car package.

Adjusted profile means were estimated using the emmeans package with HC3 covariance estimates from the sandwich package, and pairwise profile comparisons were Tukey-adjusted for the six comparisons among the four profiles within each outcome.

The present study examined how ADHD-related characteristics and self-endangering work behavior (SEWB) co-occur among workers and how they are associated with occupational well-being.
Three findings are particularly relevant.

First, participants meeting the study's ADHD criterion reported higher levels across all ten SEWB dimensions, although these associations were less consistent when ADHD was operationalized using self-reported diagnosis alone.
Second, ADHD symptoms and SEWB occurred in heterogeneous configurations that did not simply reproduce categorical ADHD group membership.

Third, individual SEWB dimensions and ADHD-SEWB profiles showed differentiated associations with burnout, work engagement, and perceived stress, with little evidence that associations between SEWB and occupational well-being differed by ADHD classification.
The higher levels of SEWB observed under the primary ADHD classification extend research on individual differences in self-endangering responses to work demands.

From a compensatory-regulation perspective, one possible interpretation is that ADHD-related difficulties in attention regulation, organization, prioritization, or time management increase the regulatory demands involved in meeting occupational goals, making additional investment of time, effort, or recovery resources more likely.

This interpretation is consistent with research documenting compensatory strategies among adults with ADHD symptoms (Kysow et al., 2017) and qualitative reports of working adults with ADHD extending work into evenings or weekends in response to difficulties encountered during regular working hours (Oscarsson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with research documenting compensatory strategies among adults with ADHD symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kysow et al., 2017)</ref> and qualitative reports of working adults with ADHD extending work into evenings or weekends in response to difficulties encountered during regular working hours <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Oscarsson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: It may be particularly relevant to resource-intensive forms of SEWB such as recovery sacrifice, working during leisure time, work intensification, and skipping breaks.
However, the present study did not assess why participants engaged in these behaviors.
Compensation may not be the only process underlying additional work investment.

Extended or intensified work could also reflect difficulty disengaging from highly engaging tasks or hyperfocus (Hupfeld et al., 2024), although evidence linking hyperfocus to burnout has so far also emerged outside occupational contexts (Pyszkowska et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Extended or intensified work could also reflect difficulty disengaging from highly engaging tasks or hyperfocus <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hupfeld et al., 2024)</ref>, although evidence linking hyperfocus to burnout has so far also emerged outside occupational contexts <ref type="bibr">(Pyszkowska et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Greater SEWB among workers meeting the ADHD criterion therefore cannot be interpreted as evidence that these behaviors represent compensation for ADHD-related difficulties.
Other processes, including difficulty disengaging from highly engaging tasks or characteristics of the work environment, may contribute to similar behavioral patterns.
At the same time, ADHD-related characteristics alone provide an incomplete account of SEWB.
The latent profiles did not reproduce categorical ADHD group membership, and similar levels of ADHD symptoms co-occurred with markedly different patterns of SEWB.

Approximately average ADHD symptoms characterized both the average symptoms/relatively low SEWB profile and the smaller quality-compromising profile, despite pronounced differences in quality deficits and concealment of performance problems.
Conversely, the elevated ADHD symptoms/broad SEWB profile combined elevated symptoms with broadly elevated self-endangering behavior.
These findings complement the categorical group differences by showing that ADHD-related characteristics are associated with SEWB without determining a uniform pattern of self-endangering behavior.
Other individual and work-related characteristics may therefore help explain why workers with similar ADHD symptom levels differ in how self-endangering behaviors are expressed.
The associations with occupational well-being further indicate that different forms of SEWB are not functionally equivalent.

Reduced exchange with colleagues and quality reduction were associated with poorer outcomes across several indicators, and quality deficits showed a particularly strong association with depersonalization.
In contrast, work intensification and working during leisure time/availability were concurrently associated with higher work engagement and lower reduced personal accomplishment.
Given the cross-sectional design, these associations should not be interpreted as evidence that resource-intensive forms of SEWB improve occupational well-being.
Rather, they indicate that self-endangering behavior can coexist with positive aspects of occupational functioning at a given point in time.

This interpretation is consistent with longitudinal evidence showing that extending and intensifying work can contribute to subsequent work stressors despite potentially supporting immediate goal attainment (Baethge et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with longitudinal evidence showing that extending and intensifying work can contribute to subsequent work stressors despite potentially supporting immediate goal attainment <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baethge et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The person-centred findings reinforce this differentiated picture.
The ADHD-SEWB profiles did not form a simple continuum from favourable to unfavourable occupational functioning.

The elevated ADHD symptoms/broad SEWB profile was characterized particularly by high perceived stress and emotional exhaustion, whereas the smaller quality-compromising profile showed high depersonalization and emotional exhaustion alongside comparatively high work engagement.
The average symptoms/relatively low SEWB profile, in turn, showed intermediate levels on several strain indicators but comparatively low work engagement.

Thus, both the variable-and person-centred findings suggest that occupational strain, engagement, ADHD symptoms, and self-endangering behavior can occur in different combinations rather than forming a single continuum of occupational functioning.
The distinctive pattern of the quality-compromising profile should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously given its small size and requires replication in independent samples.
Finally, there was little evidence that associations between individual SEWB dimensions and occupational well-being differed by ADHD classification.
None of the omnibus interaction tests remained significant after correction for multiple testing.

Within the limits of the present sample and cross-sectional design, ADHD-related characteristics may therefore be more relevant to differences in the occurrence of self-endangering behaviors than to how those behaviors are associated with burnout, work engagement, and perceived stress.
Larger samples are needed to determine whether smaller differences in these associations exist.
Several limitations should be considered.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions about temporal ordering or causality among ADHD-related characteristics, SEWB, and occupational well-being.
In particular, the positive concurrent associations of work intensification and leisure-time work with work engagement should not be interpreted as evidence of beneficial effects.
Longitudinal and intensive repeated-measures studies are needed to examine how these processes unfold over time.
Second, ADHD classification was based on self-reported diagnosis and/or a positive ASRS-6 screen rather than clinical assessment.

Moreover, associations between ADHD and individual SEWB dimensions were less consistent when ADHD was operationalized using self-reported diagnosis alone, indicating that conclusions about the breadth of these associations depend partly on ADHD operationalization.
Future studies should distinguish clinically diagnosed, screen-positive, and comparison groups while also examining ADHD symptoms dimensionally.

Third, all focal constructs were self-reported, increasing the potential for commonmethod and reporting biases, particularly for potentially sensitive behaviours such as substance use, concealment of performance problems, and quality-compromising behaviour.
Future studies could complement self-reports with repeated assessments, objective indicators, or other-source measures.
Fourth, the sample was highly educated, with more than 90% reporting a university entrance qualification, and was recruited through university participant pools.
Generalizability to other educational, occupational, employment, and sociocultural contexts is therefore uncertain.
The absence of information on several demographic characteristics further limits characterization of sample diversity.
Replication in more diverse and occupationally representative samples is needed.
Fifth, the latent profiles are sample-dependent configurations rather than fixed worker types.
In particular, the quality-compromising profile was small (n = 23; 4.9%) and requires replication before its distinctive pattern can be considered robust.

Finally, internal consistency was comparatively low for work intensification and skipping breaks, warranting caution when interpreting associations involving these dimensions and further examination of their measurement properties.
Managers should avoid diagnosis-based assumptions, as ADHD-related characteristics were associated with heterogeneous patterns of SEWB.
Rather than viewing SEWB or ADHD solely as discrete categories, managers should adopt a dimensional understanding of ADHD symptoms.
Behaviors such as sacrificing recovery, working during leisure time, skipping breaks, or concealing difficulties may signal that employees are maintaining occupational functioning at personal cost.
Managerial responses should therefore focus on the specific behavioral pattern and its work context and offer reasonable accommodation from individual needs rather than diagnosis.
The present study identifies ADHD-related characteristics as a relevant person-level correlate of SEWB.

Participants meeting the study's primary ADHD criterion reported higher levels across all forms of SEWB, while person-centred analyses showed that ADHD symptoms and SEWB co-occurred in heterogeneous configurations rather than forming a uniform pattern.

Individual forms of SEWB and ADHD-SEWB configurations were also differentially associated with occupational well-being, highlighting the importance of considering specific self-endangering behaviours rather than SEWB as a unitary pattern.

However, associations between ADHD and SEWB were less consistent when ADHD was defined by self-reported diagnosis alone, indicating that conclusions about the breadth of this association depend partly on how ADHD is operationalized.

Taken together, the findings suggest that understanding self-endangering work behavior requires attention both to ADHDrelated characteristics and to heterogeneity in the ways self-endangering patterns of working are expressed.

text.text: Beyond these average associations, ADHD-related characteristics and SEWB may occur in heterogeneous configurations across workers.
Similar levels of ADHD symptoms may coexist with different patterns of SEWB, while similar levels of SEWB may occur alongside different levels of ADHD symptoms.

Variable-centred analyses can establish average associations between ADHD-related characteristics, specific forms of SEWB, and occupational well-being, but cannot identify how these characteristics are configured within individuals.
A person-centred approach can therefore complement these analyses by identifying distinct ADHD-SEWB configurations and examining whether they differ in occupational well-being.

Accordingly, the present study combines variable-and person-centred approaches to examine associations between ADHD-related characteristics and specific forms of SEWB, identify ADHD-SEWB configurations, and examine their associations with occupational well-being.
We address in this study the following research questions: RQ1.

Is ADHD classification associated with different forms of self-endangering work behavior, and how are ADHD classification and individual SEWB dimensions associated with burnout, work engagement, and perceived stress?
RQ2.
What distinct configurations of ADHD symptoms and self-endangering work behavior can be identified among workers?
RQ3.
Do the identified ADHD-SEWB profiles differ in burnout, work engagement, and perceived stress?
Exploratory analysis: Do associations between individual SEWB dimensions and burnout, work engagement, and perceived stress differ by ADHD classification?

Standardized ADHD Symptom and Self-Endangering Work Behaviour Indicators Across the Four Latent Profiles

Profile 1, elevated ADHD symptoms/broad SEWB (n = 134; 28.5%), was characterized by elevated inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity together with broadly elevated SEWB, particularly recovery sacrifice, presenteeism, work during leisure time/availability, work intensification, and skipping breaks.
Profile 2, quality-compromising (n = 23; 4.9%), showed approximately average ADHD symptoms but markedly elevated quality deficits and concealment of performance problems.
Profile 3, low symptoms/low SEWB (n = 103; 21.9%), was characterized by low ADHD symptoms and generally low SEWB.
Profile 4, average symptoms/relatively low SEWB (n = 211; 44.8%), showed approximately average ADHD symptoms and generally low-to-average SEWB.
The profiles did not correspond directly to the categorical ADHD and comparison groups.
The proportion of participants belonging to the ADHD group was 67.9% in Profile 1, 30.4% in Profile 2, 3.9% in Profile 3, and 35.1% in Profile 4.
Thus, the profiles reflected variation in the joint configuration of continuous ADHD symptoms and SEWB rather than reproducing the categorical ADHD grouping.
